content: Cost-effectiveness modeling studies were evaluated for their overall quality by examining the structure of the model, the appropriateness of the assumptions, the sources of model inputs, and the sensitivity analyses conducted. However, a formal quality assessment tool was not utilized. Most studies employed a state transition model (Markov model) with variable cycle lengths ranging from one month to one year and time horizons varying from one year to a lifetime (up to 95 years of age). Nearly all studies were conducted from a payer or health system perspective. The majority of studies did not use systematic reviews to identify the most appropriate model inputs, and the methods for selecting studies for utility inputs were rarely described. Most studies included one-way sensitivity analyses, while some also performed multi-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses. A key assumption influencing outcomes in some studies was that single-pill combinations improved compliance, leading to better blood pressure control. Costs associated with adverse events were included in some studies but not in others. Although some studies extensively described their models and assumptions, the lack of systematic reviews for input selection introduced potential bias. The generalizability of these studies was limited due to contextual differences. For example, Gu and colleagues assessed the cost-effectiveness of low-cost essential antihypertensive medications for hypertension control in China using a state transition model. They calculated the cost-effectiveness of treating stage 1 (BP 140–159/90–99 mmHg) and stage 2 (BP ≥160/100 mmHg) hypertension. Both one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted. Treating hypertensive adults with prior cardiovascular disease for secondary prevention was found to be cost-saving in the main simulation and in 100% of probabilistic simulation results. Treatment of other patient cohorts, including sensitivity analyses, was cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of USD 50,000. Data from 4,500 US adults with hypertension from the Community Quality Index study were modeled to estimate the cost and cost-effectiveness of consistently providing the basic elements of blood pressure management (visits and medications associated with recommended care). They compared usual care with improved care, which involved 100% provision of recommended care processes. Some inputs were derived from systematic reviews or meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials. Improved care was estimated to cost USD 170 per person annually for mild hypertension, USD 801 for moderate hypertension, and USD 850 for severe hypertension. Park and colleagues conducted a systematic review of cost-effectiveness analyses of antihypertensive medications, including 76 studies. These studies compared medications with no treatment, conventional treatment, other medication classes, medications within the same class, and different combination therapies. Quality assessment was performed using the Quality of Health Economic Studies scale, with 21 studies scoring above 91 and 10 studies scoring below 70 on a 100-point scale. Industry funding accounted for 80% of reported funding, and these studies often provided favorable evidence for the sponsoring companies. Most studies originated from Europe (41 studies), followed by North America (16 studies), and other countries (19 studies). Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) were the most frequently evaluated drug class, appearing 62 times as either an intervention or comparator in 42 studies. Losartan and irbesartan were the most commonly included ARBs. Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) were the next most frequently evaluated class, with amlodipine being the most common drug. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) and beta-blockers (BBs) were also frequently studied, with atenolol being the most common beta-blocker. Thiazide diuretics were evaluated 17 times, with hydrochlorothiazide being the most frequent. All antihypertensives were cost-effective compared to no treatment, with ARBs being more cost-effective than CCBs in nine comparisons, while CCBs were more cost-effective than ARBs in two comparisons. ARBs were consistently more cost-effective than ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers in all comparisons. Variations in study results were attributed to differences in study settings, analytic models, cost variations, and potential publication bias. Tajeu and colleagues studied the cost-effectiveness of antihypertensive medications in white and black men and women in the United States using a state transition model. The simulation population was modeled using demographic and clinical data from the REGARDS study, which examines risk factors associated with stroke. Health states included stroke, coronary heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and end-stage kidney disease. Antihypertensive treatment was found to be cost-effective with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) exceeding USD 1,000 for all groups. In an economic analysis funded by Novartis, benazepril was evaluated for patients with chronic kidney disease using data from the AIPRI study for transition probabilities. Benazepril was found to be dominant over a seven-year time horizon. Gad and colleagues conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis in Ghana using a state transition model with six health states, one-year cycle lengths, and a lifetime time horizon. They compared the cost-effectiveness of different medication classes, including ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, CCBs, thiazide-like diuretics, and no intervention. Thiazide diuretics were the most cost-effective option, followed by CCBs, while ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers were less effective than thiazide diuretics. These results were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Ekwunife and colleagues conducted a cost-utility analysis of antihypertensive medications in Nigeria using a Markov model with six health states, one-year cycle lengths, and a 30-year time horizon. Thiazide diuretics were the most cost-effective option across cardiovascular risk groups, followed by CCBs, at a willingness-to-pay threshold of at least USD 2,000 per QALY. The results were robust and insensitive to parameter alterations. An industry-sponsored cost-utility analysis comparing eprosartan with enalapril and nitrendipine found eprosartan to be cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of EUR 30,000. Another industry-funded study from Taiwan comparing amlodipine and valsartan found amlodipine to be dominant, with results robust in sensitivity analyses. A non-industry-funded study in Poland comparing ACE inhibitors and ARBs found ACE inhibitors to provide improved outcomes compared to ARBs, with significant gains in QALYs and life-years. An economic evaluation sponsored by Daiichi-Sankyo in China used a well-designed Markov model to analyze the cost-effectiveness of olmesartan/amlodipine single-pill combinations compared to multiple-pill combinations. The single-pill combination was found to be dominant. Similarly, a single-pill combination of indapamide and amlodipine was cost-saving in a Polish setting. Lung et al. compared the cost-effectiveness of a triple-pill strategy (amlodipine, telmisartan, and chlorthalidone) with usual care using a discrete-time simulation model. The triple-pill strategy was cost-effective, with findings robust to variations in key parameters. Equity issues were highlighted in low-income countries, where health insurance often does not cover newer-generation medications. Patients face challenges such as inconsistent prescribing practices and short prescription durations, which increase treatment costs and reduce compliance. In black patients, there is limited high-quality data on the effectiveness of ACE inhibitors or ARBs, but subgroup analyses suggest higher cardiovascular risks compared to other antihypertensives. Increasing treatment rates and adherence among black adults could address racial disparities in care. Factors such as distrust in the healthcare system and alternative beliefs about hypertension may influence adherence in African American populations. Simplified dosing regimens and single-pill combinations improve adherence but may limit flexibility in dose adjustments.
